title: With friends
goal: Say who you're with, what you use, and what you do for a living — and complete the sixth and final case: the instrumental, the only one often used with no preposition at all.
bekal: use *s* + instrumental to say who you're with
use the instrumental without a preposition for tools and vehicles
say what you do for a living and ask others about their jobs

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Čím sa živíš?
dialogs.intro: At a birthday party. Budi meets Eva's friend, a man called Marek.

lines.speaker: Marek:
lines.text: Ahoj, ja som Marek. Ty si ten Indonézan?
lines.id: Hi, I'm Marek. Are you the Indonesian guy?
lines.literal: hello, I I-am Marek. you you-are that Indonesian-man?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Áno, Budi. Prišiel som s Evou.
lines.id: Yes, Budi. I came with Eva.

lines.text: Poznám ju od strednej školy. A čím sa živíš?

lines.literal: interesting. I I-am teacher-ins at grammar-school-loc.

lines.speaker: Marek:
lines.text: Chodím s rodinou do Chorvátska. Autom, dva dni.

lines.literal: I-go with family-ins to Croatia-gen. car-ins, two days-pl.

notes: **S Evou, s rodinou, s tímom** — the preposition *s* always takes the instrumental, and it means "with" (together). Notice that there is a preposition written here; this is the instrumental's first job.

**Perom, autom — no preposition at all.** This is the second job, and the most distinctive: tools and vehicles are expressed with a **bare** instrumental ending. *Píšem perom* = I write with a pen. There's no word for "with" in the sentence; the ending says it.

**So *s* and the bare instrumental must not be mixed up.** *Píšem perom* = I write with a pen (a tool). *Píšem s Evou* = I write together with Eva (a companion). Add *s* to a tool and the sentence sounds odd: *píšem s perom* sounds as if the pen is writing alongside you.

**Som učiteľom** uses the instrumental for a job, and that's fine — but *som učiteľ* with the basic form is also correct and heard more often. The difference is subtle: the instrumental stresses the role or position a little more, the basic form stresses identity. At A1, use the basic form and recognize the other.
**Čím sa živíš?** literally "what do you feed yourself with?" — a friendly, slightly casual way to ask about someone's job. More neutral: *Čo robíš?* or *Kde pracuješ?*

grammars.title: The instrumental — the sixth and final case
body: The instrumental answers the questions *kým?* (with whom) and *čím?* (with what). Its endings are the most uniform of all six cases: practically just two forms.
after: **Two endings for the whole system: *-om* and *-ou*.** Masculine and neuter take *-om*; feminine takes *-ou*. No animate/inanimate split, no exceptions to learn at A1. After the previous five cases, this feels like a gift.

**Adjectives**: m and n take **-ým** (*s dobrým bratom*, *pod veľkým stolom*), f takes **-ou** (*s dobrou sestrou*). Notice that feminine adjectives take the same ending as the noun — the only case where the two rhyme.

**Instrumental pronouns**: *mnou, tebou, ním, ňou, nami, vami, nimi*. All long, all can stand anywhere, and almost always preceded by a preposition: *so mnou*, *s tebou*, *s ním*, *s ňou*, *s nami*, *s vami*, *s nimi*.

grammars.title: The four jobs of the instrumental
body: This case has four clearly different jobs, and you've already been using three of them since the early units without explanation.
after: **The rule that covers it all: if what's with you is a person, use *s*. If it's a tool, a vehicle, or a means, use nothing.** A simple check: could the thing "come along" of its own free will? If not, it's a tool.
**S becomes so** before words starting with *s, z, š, ž* and before *mnou*: *so sestrou*, *so Zuzanou*, *so mnou*. Just like *v/vo*, *z/zo*, *k/ku*.

**Four prepositions of position — *pred, za, nad, pod* — take the instrumental for rest and the accusative for motion.** *Auto stojí pred domom* (the car is parked in front of the house, rest, instrumental) but *Idem pred dom* (I'm going in front of the house, motion, accusative). You met the same split between motion and rest in units 6 and 11.

blocks.text: Once again the ending **-ka** forms the female partner, with small sound adjustments: *-ník → -níčka*, *-vač → -vačka*. Once you know the male form, you practically get the female one for free — the same pattern as unit 3.

head: Questions and answers
English

blocks.title: Dôchodca: one word that says a lot
items: *Dôchodcovia* (pensioners) are a very visible group in everyday Slovak life: they get big discounts on trains and city transport, and mornings on trams and at markets are mostly theirs.
Giving up your seat to an older person on the tram isn't extra politeness — it's a firm expectation, and if you don't, strangers around you will tell you off out loud.

blocks.text: Look at the eighth and ninth rows: **talking and meeting take *s***, because the person you talk to is a person, not a tool. *Hovorím s lekárom*, not *hovorím lekárom*. This mistake turns up precisely because the tool rule has already stuck.

blocks.title: Six cases, done
items: With this unit you've used all six Slovak cases: nominative (unit 1), accusative (4), locative (6), genitive (9), dative (10), instrumental (17).

The full table is on the *A1 Grammar Summary* page at the back of this book. But if you've got here by working through every unit, you're not memorizing that table — you're recognizing something you've already been using.
